query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 FCC HEA, the degradation under elevated temperature is governed by the interplay between microstructural grain-boundary networks (inherent to additive manufacturing) and gas chemistry. Under oxidizing atmospheres, rapid diffusion along high-density grain boundaries promotes the formation of a continuous, protective Cr-/Al-rich outer oxide scale that preserves mechanical integrity. In contrast, under reducing (or alternating reducing) atmospheres, limited external oxygen causes the grain-boundary channels to act as fast internal diffusion paths, triggering internal oxidation that forms sub-scale voids and disrupts the oxide scale adhesion, leading to accelerated degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with a predominantly FCC matrix and a high density of grain boundaries and defects typical for AM-produced microstructures.
generation.intervention: Expose identical samples to controlled high-temperature (around 900 °C) environments under well-defined atmospheres: one set under continuously oxidizing gas conditions and another set under alternating oxidizing and reducing gas cycles.
generation.conditions: Temperature maintained at ~900 °C for durations up to 100 hours with precise control over gas partial pressures (e.g., oxygen-rich vs oxygen-lean/reducing conditions), ensuring that oxidation kinetics are compared under steady and cyclic conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The additive manufacturing–induced ultrafine grain structure with an extensive network of grain boundaries mediating rapid diffusion of both oxygen and alloying elements.
generation.mechanism: In an oxygen-rich atmosphere, the grain-boundary diffusion quickly supplies Cr and Al to the surface, forming a well-adherent, layered oxide scale (with a Cr2O3/Al2O3 inner layer) that slows further oxidation. Under reducing gas exposure, the limited external oxygen reduces the formation of the protective outer scale and instead favors internal oxidation along the grain boundaries, causing void formation and scale undercutting which ultimately compromises adhesion and accelerates mechanical degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exposed solely to oxidizing conditions will exhibit a continuous and protective oxide scale with low internal damage and minimal spallation, while samples subjected to reducing or alternating oxidizing/reducing cycles will display evidence of internal oxidation (e.g., grain-boundary voids, sub-scale degradation) and a less coherent outer oxide layer, correlating with increased mass gain and decreased mechanical integrity.
generation.baseline: The as-manufactured AM alloy exhibiting its initial protective oxide formation mechanism under standard oxidizing conditions versus conventional cast or wrought alloys (where microstructure is coarser and grain-boundary effects are less pronounced).
generation.boundary: This mechanistic explanation applies specifically to the AM-produced FCC high-entropy alloy at elevated temperatures (~900 °C) and may not hold for substantially different alloy compositions, processing routes that yield different microstructures, or temperature regimes where alternative oxidation kinetics prevail.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis extends the layered oxidation findings (as described in PMC11169556::web::016::results_and_discussion) and the role of microstructural refinement enhancing oxidation resistance (PMC9026100::web::004::introduction) to the unique grain-boundary network produced by AM. Uncertainties remain regarding the relative oxidation contributions of minor elements (such as Ti) and the exact balance between internal versus external oxidation in these complex gas environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple samples of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA and subject them to two controlled oxidation protocols: (1) a continuous oxidizing atmosphere at 900 °C and (2) an alternating cycle of oxidizing and reducing gases under the same temperature and total exposure time. After testing, perform detailed oxide scale and microstructure characterization through cross-sectional TEM, atom probe tomography (APT), and measurements of mass gain and mechanical properties (e.g., microhardness, adhesion tests). Compare the continuity, composition, and integrity of the oxide scale as well as evidence of internal oxidation.
measurements: Oxide scale morphology and thickness (via TEM and SEM)
Detection and mapping of internal oxide penetration along grain boundaries (using APT)
Residual mechanical properties (e.g., hardness, tensile strength) after exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples subjected to reducing/alternating gas cycles do not show significantly increased internal oxidation (e.g., similar oxide scale continuity, negligible presence of grain-boundary voids, and comparable mechanical properties) relative to the continuous oxidizing samples, then the proposed mechanism—that the AM-induced grain-boundary network triggers detrimental internal oxidation under reducing conditions—would be falsified.

From this study, we conclude the following: the oxide scale in HEAs is a function of their complex chemistries and microstructures. We addressed the problem piecewise, studying the oxidation of a single crystal HEA without the microstructural complications and defects to understand the role of alloy chemistry. Subsequently, we considered numerous microstructural features, including compositional segregations observed experimentally, to understand the scale growth in different microstructural regions. We have not yet addressed the problem of internal oxidation using CA. Our future efforts will focus on understanding internal oxidation and subsequently integrate the individual simulations for modeling the microstructures of oxidized HEAs.
